name: Silver oxide
plain: A single-use 1.55-volt button battery used in quartz watches and small precision devices. It holds a steady voltage until it is used up, and the silver makes it costly.
self_discharge: Over 90% of service retained after 5 years at 21 °C (Energizer)
summary: Silver oxide button batteries pair a zinc anode with a silver oxide cathode in an alkaline electrolyte and hold a nearly constant 1.55 V until depleted. They are the SR batteries used in quartz watches and precision miniature electronics.
body:
## How it works

A silver oxide battery, IEC system S, uses silver(I) oxide as the cathode and powdered zinc as the anode, in an alkaline electrolyte of sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide. In the common button form, Wikipedia describes a graphite-infused silver oxide cathode at the bottom of the battery, separated by a plastic membrane from the zinc anode. Energizer's construction notes list molded nylon gaskets and nickel exterior surfaces, which resist corrosion and give good electrical contact. The silver is reduced from Ag(I) to Ag and the zinc oxidized from Zn to Zn(II). Silver is expensive, which is why the chemistry is sold almost entirely in small button sizes.

## Discharge behavior

Open-circuit voltage is 1.6 V and the operating voltage at typical drains is 1.55 V or more. The discharge curve is flatter than alkaline manganese dioxide, and internal resistance is low and essentially constant. Energizer reports over 90% service maintenance after five years at 21 °C.

The electrolyte sets the drain rating. Energizer recommends potassium hydroxide batteries for heavier drains, such as LCD watches with backlights and alarms, where they last about one to two years, and sodium hydroxide batteries for low drains, such as analog watches, for up to five years. Batteries can be used up to 55 °C; potassium hydroxide batteries operate down to −28 °C and sodium hydroxide batteries down to −10 °C, with reduced service in both.

## Uses

Watches, calculators, cameras and other precision miniature electronics. IEC 60086-3 defines a coding system for watch batteries; Wikipedia's summary lists the suffixes P (potassium hydroxide electrolyte), S (sodium hydroxide electrolyte), SW (low-drain type for quartz watches without light, alarm or chronograph) and W (high-drain type that meets all of IEC 60086-3), as in SR626SW. Wikipedia reports that silver oxide batteries were 30% of single-use battery sales in Japan in February 2020.

## History

Large silver oxide batteries flew on early ICBMs and satellites, including the Corona reconnaissance satellites, and later in the Apollo Lunar Module and lunar rover. Until 2004, all silver oxide batteries contained up to 0.2% mercury in the zinc anode to inhibit corrosion; Sony began producing the first mercury-free silver oxide batteries in 2004. The EU exemption that allowed button batteries up to 2% mercury by weight ended on October 1, 2015.

## Status

Current. IEC 60086-1 lists system S at 1.55 V nominal with a 1.63 V maximum open-circuit voltage.
strengths: Higher voltage than comparable mercury batteries (Energizer)
limitations: Silver makes it costly, so it is sold almost only in button sizes
Low-drain (SW) batteries are not rated for backlights or alarms
safety: Button battery ingestion hazard: swallowed batteries can cause severe internal burns
Leakage can occur at temperatures of 100 °C or more (Wikipedia)
